claims.text: Wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by dynamic grain-boundary stabilization.
Controlled grain-boundary segregation or precipitation forms a protective phase during wear.
Low-temperature annealing that enhances grain-boundary segregation will improve wear resistance relative to the as-deposited condition.
The relevant as-deposited coatings are nanocrystalline or multiphase and lack significant pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates.
A suitable low-temperature annealing treatment can selectively induce grain-boundary segregation or precipitation without substantially changing grain size or bulk composition.
Under the proposed wear conditions, the coating microstructure remains intact and only grain-boundary chemistry is modified.
Annealing produces segregated elements or fine precipitates along grain boundaries.
The modified grain-boundary chemistry promotes nucleation of a protective surface phase during wear.
Controlled grain-boundary segregation or precipitation dynamically stabilizes the grain boundaries.
The in situ protective phase resists crack initiation.
The in situ protective phase resists abrasive wear.
Annealed coatings will have lower wear volume or wear rate than as-deposited coatings.
Annealed coatings may have a lower friction coefficient or improved durability relative to as-deposited coatings.
The wear improvement will occur while grain size and bulk hardness remain similar to those of the as-deposited baseline.
The hypothesis applies only to annealing conditions that modify grain-boundary chemistry without causing grain growth or significant bulk phase transformation.
